Female Alpine river galaxias, or Galaxias paucispondylus, ultimately attain a maximum body length of 11.2 centimeters [Li = 11.2 centimeters], a modest size that reflects the energetic constraints of high-altitude stream habitats. This ultimate total length represents a considerable investment of resources in somatic growth before reproductive effort begins in earnest. Field surveys conducted throughout the South Island river systems consistently report that females reach this asymptotic dimension only after several years of steady feeding and favorable thermal conditions, highlighting the species' slow-paced life history relative to lowland galaxiids.

Sexual maturation in female Alpine river galaxias is initiated once individuals reach a total length of 7 centimeters [Lp = 7 centimeters], a threshold that typically corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis. This length at puberty is relatively small compared to some congeneric species, suggesting that Galaxias paucispondylus may adopt an earlier reproductive strategy to compensate for elevated adult mortality in its unpredictable alpine environment. Gonadal development proceeds rapidly after this size is attained, with females becoming capable of spawning within a single growing season.

At a stable water temperature of 8 °C [T = 8 °C], reproductive output in Galaxias paucispondylus has been quantified under controlled laboratory conditions. Females produce an average of 278 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 278 eggs per spawning event] and typically complete one such event each year [F_R_i = one such event each year], yielding an annual reproductive rate of approximately 278 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 278 eggs per year]. This annual reproductive schedule is tightly coupled with the spring snowmelt cycle, which provides stable thermal conditions near 8 °C that are essential for optimal oocyte development and gamete maturation.

Newly hatched larvae of Alpine river galaxias emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs measuring approximately 2.2 millimeters in diameter. The wet weight at birth for these yolk-sac larvae is just 0.0056 grams [Wwb = just 0.0056 grams], an extremely low mass that underscores the high degree of endotrophic reliance during the early free-swimming phase. This minimal initial body mass forces a rapid exotrophic transition; within days of chorion rupture, the prolarvae must successfully capture their first prey to avoid starvation, placing a critical bottleneck on early survival in the oligotrophic alpine streams they inhabit.

Under controlled conditions at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], Galaxias paucispondylus exhibits a maximum recorded longevity of approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years]. This lifespan is notably extended when compared with smaller-bodied galaxiids, likely reflecting the lower metabolic costs associated with the cooler thermal regime of its natural habitat. Wild populations probably exhibit somewhat shorter lifespans due to predation pressure and seasonal resource limitation, though direct field validation remains scarce.
